zero-carb-carnivore.summary: Eating only animal foods to get leaner, hold muscle and, followers say, clear skin through a high-protein, appetite-lowering routine.

quick.overview:
The zero-carb carnivore diet allows only animal foods such as meat, fish, eggs and sometimes dairy, with no plants and no added carbohydrate. People follow it to drop fat, keep muscle and, they report, calm skin and inflammation.

The chain is high protein and fat, which keeps appetite low, so intake falls and the body gets leaner; with almost no carbohydrate the body usually runs on fat and ketones. Shawn Baker and the Petersons helped popularise it from about 2017 to 2019. Published data consist of a 2021 self-selected survey, case reports and small series.
quick.how: Meals are built from beef, fish, eggs and sometimes dairy, with trace carbohydrate from animal sources accepted. Followers often eat to appetite rather than counting calories, and some use it as a strict reset, then keep or loosen it. Users commonly report changes in weight and digestion within weeks.
quick.risks: Reported or discussed risks include no fibre, possible shortfalls of vitamin C and other micronutrients, sharply raised LDL cholesterol in some people, constipation, gout and kidney strain. The British Dietetic Association and Dietitians Australia classify it as a fad diet, and long-term safety has not been established.

angle.text: Followers eat only animal foods so high protein keeps appetite down, body fat drops and muscle is held, with clearer skin and less inflammation reported along the way. The support is mainly self-reported surveys and case reports.

ribeye-and-water-carnivore.summary: The strictest carnivore routine, fatty steak and water, used for a simple, filling path to a leaner body and clearer skin.

quick.overview:
Ribeye and water is shorthand for a very narrow carnivore diet where fatty beef steak is the main or only food. People use it to take decisions out of eating, aiming for leanness, muscle and clearer skin.

The chain is that a fatty, protein-rich steak is filling and the menu is so limited that intake stays simple and predictable. Carnivore advocates recommend fatty cuts such as ribeye, 80/20 ground beef and added tallow so most calories come from fat. It is not a separately studied protocol; the research that exists covers the wider carnivore diet and is mostly self-reports.
quick.how: Meals are steak, sometimes with ground beef or tallow, and water. People typically use it as a short, strict stretch or a base for broader carnivore eating, and report on appetite and digestion within the first weeks.
quick.risks: Concerns raised for the wider carnivore diet include fibre and micronutrient gaps, a documented scurvy case on mostly canned beef, raised LDL cholesterol, constipation, gout and kidney strain.

angle.text: Followers cut eating down to fatty beef and water so meals stay filling and simple, aiming for a leaner body, muscle and clearer skin. It is an informal shorthand within carnivore eating, and studies cover the wider carnivore diet rather than this version.

carnivore-ish-animal-based-diet.summary: Paul Saladino's looser carnivore diet of meat, organs, fruit, honey and raw dairy, followed for clearer skin, energy and a leaner physique.

quick.overview:
The animal-based diet centres on ruminant meat, organ meats, fish, eggs and often raw dairy, with limited fruit and honey for carbohydrate, and no vegetables, grains, legumes, nuts or seeds. People follow it for clearer skin, better sleep and energy, and a leaner physique.

The chain is nutrient-dense animal foods, with fruit and honey adding energy, so eating stays simple while nutrient needs are covered. Psychiatrist Paul Saladino popularised it in the early 2020s as a looser form of strict carnivore, after reporting low energy, poor sleep and low testosterone on strict carnivore. Short-term feeding research shows an all-animal diet changes gut bacteria within days, and no trial has tested the full pattern. Looksmax.org users post both enthusiastic essays and reports of poor sleep, fatigue and acne after a year.
quick.how: Plates are built around beef, organ meats, eggs and fish, with fruit and honey for carbohydrate and sometimes raw dairy. Many people treat it as an easier version of carnivore, and report changes in digestion and energy over weeks to months.
quick.risks: Concerns raised include missing fibre and plant nutrients, high saturated fat, and the food-safety risk of raw dairy. Mainstream nutrition experts call the diet restrictive.

angle.text: Followers eat meat, organs, fruit and honey for clearer skin, better sleep, energy and a leaner physique, on the idea that nutrient-dense animal foods cover their needs. Evidence is mostly testimonials, and no trial has tested the whole pattern.

raw-egg-consumption.summary: Drinking raw eggs in shakes as cheap protein and choline for muscle gain, Rocky-style, with Salmonella and lower protein absorption to weigh.

quick.overview:
Raw egg consumption means drinking or eating uncooked eggs, usually blended into shakes, as a cheap protein and choline source for building muscle. It follows the old strongman and Rocky Balboa image and appears on looksmax.org forums.

The chain is protein and choline intake supporting training and muscle gain. Wikipedia reports egg protein is about 51 percent bioavailable raw versus roughly 91 percent cooked, so less of the protein is absorbed raw. Forum posts range from people drinking a dozen or more at a time to threads calling raw eggs a meme.
quick.how: Eggs are blended with milk, banana or protein powder into a shake, usually around training. Some users choose pasteurised eggs. Any muscle effect would arrive through overall protein intake and training over months.
quick.risks: Salmonella can contaminate eggs inside the egg or on a cracked shell, and heat destroys it; case-control research found raw eggs a leading risk factor for Salmonella Enteritidis infection. Health authorities advise vulnerable groups against raw eggs. Raw egg white contains avidin, which binds biotin, and raw egg allergy reactions have been reported even in people who tolerate cooked egg. Pasteurised eggs are sold as a lower-risk option.

angle.text: Raw eggs go into shakes as inexpensive protein and choline to support training and muscle gain. Research reports lower protein absorption from raw eggs than cooked, and no studies look at appearance.

liver-organ-meats-beef-liver.summary: Beef liver, an unusually nutrient-dense food rich in vitamin A, B12 and iron, eaten by forum users for skin and vitality.

quick.overview:
Beef liver is rich in preformed vitamin A, vitamin B12, riboflavin, copper and iron, and in looksmaxxing and ancestral-diet circles it is eaten as a whole-food alternative to multivitamins for skin, energy and general vitality.

The chain is that nutrients concentrated in liver support skin, hair and energy. The nutrient content is well documented in reference sources; no published human trial has tested liver for skin, facial appearance or attractiveness.
quick.how: People cook it as slices or pan-fried pieces, mix it into ground beef, or take it frozen in small pieces. Forum members disagree about eating it raw, frozen or cooked, and many eat it as an occasional food rather than daily.
quick.risks: A single serving of liver can exceed the adult tolerable upper intake level of 3,000 micrograms per day of preformed vitamin A. Excess preformed vitamin A is associated with headaches, liver damage, bone effects and, in pregnancy, harm to the fetus, and health agencies advise limits, especially in pregnancy. Raw liver carries the food-safety concerns of any raw meat.

angle.text: Forum users eat beef liver for its vitamin A, B12 and iron, expecting healthier skin and more vitality. Its nutrient content is well documented; trials on appearance have not been done.

desiccated-organ-supplements-beef-organs.summary: Freeze-dried beef liver and organ capsules taken as a convenient stand-in for organ meats, for skin, energy and general nutrition.

quick.overview:
Desiccated organ supplements are capsules or powders made from dried beef liver and sometimes heart, kidney or spleen. They are taken to get organ-meat nutrients without cooking or tasting them, for skin, energy and general nutrition, and are marketed as a multivitamin alternative.

The chain is that the capsules deliver what the source organ contains, mainly in liver preformed vitamin A, B12, riboflavin, iron and copper. Reference sources confirm organ meats are nutrient-dense; no published trial was found testing these capsules for skin, hair, energy or appearance.
quick.how: People take capsules or stir powder into food as a daily supplement alongside, or in place of, eating organ meats. Products are often combined into liver-plus-other-organ blends, and users report on energy and skin over weeks to months.
quick.risks: Liver-derived products contain preformed vitamin A, for which health sources list a tolerable upper intake level of 3,000 micrograms per day for adults, with limits advised in pregnancy. Dietary supplements are not regulated like drugs, and content and quality vary by manufacturer.

angle.text: Dried organ capsules are taken as an easy way to get liver and organ nutrients, hoping for better skin, energy and general nutrition. The nutrient profile of the source organs is documented; no appearance trials exist for the capsules.

bone-marrow-bone-broth.summary: Slow-simmered bones and marrow, consumed for collagen to support firmer skin and healthier joints.

quick.overview:
Bone broth is stock made by simmering bones and connective tissue for a long time; bone marrow is the fatty tissue inside long bones, eaten roasted or in soups. Both are used in wellness and looksmaxxing circles for collagen, with users hoping for firmer skin and healthier joints.

The chain is that simmering releases collagen, which turns into gelatin, supplying collagen building blocks for skin and joints. Bone broth became a wellness trend in the early 2010s; Wikipedia reports there is no scientific evidence to support many of the claims made for it, and no published trial was found testing it for skin or appearance.
quick.how: Broth is simmered for hours with bones, vegetables and herbs and drunk as a warm drink or used as a soup base; marrow is roasted and eaten on bread or stirred into dishes. Users often make it a regular daily or weekly habit.
quick.risks: Broth and marrow are ordinary foods generally not regarded as risky for most people. Marrow is high in fat, and bones can concentrate contaminants in some preparations. Vertebral spinal marrow is banned for sale in some countries, including the UK, because of mad cow disease concerns.

angle.text: Bone broth and marrow are consumed for their collagen, with users hoping for firmer skin and healthier joints. Both are long-standing foods, and no published trials examine appearance.

beef-tallow.summary: Rendered beef fat used as a cooking fat and, lately, as a face moisturiser for softer, less dry-looking skin.

quick.overview:
Beef tallow is beef fat rendered into a solid. It has long been used for frying, soap and candles, and has become popular in ancestral-diet and looksmaxxing communities as a cooking fat and as a moisturiser rubbed on the skin.

The chain is that as food it is a calorie-dense fat from a simple source, and on skin fats generally act as occlusives that slow water loss, leaving skin softer. Tallow is roughly 50 percent saturated and 42 percent monounsaturated fat. No published human trial was found testing it for skin or appearance, and Wikipedia describes some claims that it is healthier than seed oils as unscientific.
quick.how: People fry and roast with it in place of seed oils, and apply small amounts to the face as a balm, often at night. Users report on skin feel within days to weeks.
quick.risks: As food, tallow is high in saturated fat and cholesterol, and older diet studies found saturated fats raise serum cholesterol. Topical use has no published safety data, and moisturisers in general can cause contact dermatitis in some people.

angle.text: Beef tallow is used in ancestral-diet cooking and applied to the face as a moisturiser, aiming for softer, less dry-looking skin. As a fat it would be expected to hold moisture in; no trials have tested its skin effects.

tallow-skincare.summary: Rendered beef fat, often whipped into a balm, applied to the face as a simple moisturiser for softer, less dry-looking skin.

quick.overview:
Tallow skincare means using rendered beef fat, alone or blended into balms, as a face and body moisturiser. It spread through ancestral-diet and wellness communities as part of a move toward traditional, minimally processed fats, and users choose it over conventional creams.

The chain is that fats and oils on skin generally act as occlusives, forming a layer that slows water loss, which leaves skin softer and less dry-looking. Proponents say tallow's fatty acid profile resembles human skin oils. No published trial was found testing tallow on skin.
quick.how: People rub a small amount of whipped tallow balm onto the face, often after cleansing or at night, and some blend it with other oils. Users report on how skin feels within days to weeks.
quick.risks: There are no published safety studies for tallow as a skin product. Moisturisers in general can cause contact dermatitis in some users, and animal fats can go rancid or carry contaminants depending on preparation.

angle.text: Users apply whipped tallow balm to the face as a moisturiser, preferring a simple animal-fat product to conventional creams. Fats on skin slow water loss, which is the route to softer skin; published trials on tallow itself are lacking.

raw-honey-bee-pollen.summary: Hive products eaten or applied for clearer skin and energy; honey has wound-care evidence, bee pollen's health benefits are described as unproven.

quick.overview:
Raw honey is honey that has not been heated or pasteurised, and bee pollen is the pollen pellets bees collect as food. In wellness and looksmaxxing circles both are used for clearer skin, energy and testosterone.

The chain is that honey has antibacterial activity that varies between honeys, and bee pollen supplies sugars, protein, minerals and vitamins. Honey has preliminary evidence for faster healing of some wounds and burns. Wikipedia describes bee pollen's health benefits as unproven, and no published trial was found testing either product for skin appearance or testosterone in healthy people.
quick.how: Honey is eaten by the spoonful, stirred into drinks or applied to skin as a mask; bee pollen granules are sprinkled on yogurt or smoothies. Users typically add them to a daily routine and report on skin over weeks.
quick.risks: Bee pollen can cause allergic reactions in people allergic to pollen, from hives to anaphylaxis, may be contaminated with mycotoxins, pesticides or metals, and is not considered safe in pregnancy. Honey can carry Clostridium botulinum spores and is not recommended for infants under one year. The FDA has warned about bee pollen products adulterated with unapproved drugs.

angle.text: Raw honey and bee pollen are used for clearer skin and for testosterone, on the idea that their nutrients and antibacterial properties help. Honey has some wound-care evidence; no trials test either product for appearance.

fruitarian-diet.summary: Eating mainly fruit for clear, glowing skin and a lean body, with case reports describing nutritional problems.

quick.overview:
A fruitarian diet is built mainly or wholly on fruit, sometimes with nuts and seeds. Some people in appearance communities follow it for clean, glowing skin and a lean body.

The chain is that fruit is water-rich and low in calories, followers remove processed foods and animal products, and the antioxidant-containing produce is thought to improve skin while weight comes down. No clinical trial has tested it for appearance; the published literature consists of case reports, including a type 1 diabetes patient, a case of reversible dementia and a leukemia patient who combined it with long fasts.
quick.how: Meals are fresh fruit, sometimes with nuts and seeds, and practitioners differ on what counts as fruit and what else is allowed. People try it for periods ranging from days to long term and report on skin and weight within weeks.
quick.risks: Dietitians cite possible shortfalls of vitamin B12, protein, calcium, iron, zinc and vitamin D, a high sugar load, and unsuitability for children and pregnant or nursing women. Case reports include reversible dementia and altered glucose control in type 1 diabetes.

angle.text: Some people eat only fruit hoping for clean, glowing skin and a lean body, through a light, low-calorie intake. No appearance trials exist, and published case reports focus on nutritional problems.

raw-vegan-diet.summary: Eating only uncooked plant foods for better skin, leanness and general health.

quick.overview:
A raw vegan diet is made of uncooked plant foods such as fruit, vegetables, nuts, seeds and sprouts, kept below roughly 40-49 degrees Celsius. People in appearance communities follow it for better skin and leanness.

The chain is high fibre and a lot of produce, with processed food off the menu, which followers say leads to clearer skin and a leaner body. Proponents say heat destroys enzymes and nutrients; dietetic sources say cooking does not simply destroy nutrients and can improve availability of some. Research is small observational studies and case reports, and none examined appearance.
quick.how: Meals are salads, smoothies, sprouts, nut-based dishes and dehydrated foods. Followers often prepare food in bulk and report changes in weight and skin within weeks to months.
quick.risks: Reported concerns include low B12, vitamin D and calories, and case reports describe problems in children.

angle.text: Followers eat only uncooked plant foods for the fibre and produce intake, hoping for better skin, leanness and general health. Small studies cover nutrition status and none cover looks; B12 intake is a recurring topic.

vegan-diet.summary: Plant-only eating used for leanness and skin, with trial data on weight and cardiometabolic markers; B12 must come from fortified foods or supplements.

quick.overview:
A vegan diet excludes all animal products. In appearance circles it is used for leanness and skin, and in some anecdotal claims for lighter eye colour.

The chain is that vegan diets are higher in fibre and lower in saturated fat and shift gut microbiota, and trials of low-fat vegan diets report weight loss and better glycemic control and cardiovascular risk factors, which feeds into a leaner body. Skin effects are claimed rather than studied, and no trials examine looks.
quick.how: People build meals from legumes, grains, vegetables, fruit, nuts and soy products, and take B12 from fortified foods or supplements. Weight changes appear over weeks to months, and many pair the diet with training.
quick.risks: The main concern is vitamin B12, which comes only from fortified foods or supplements, plus vitamin D, calcium, iodine, iron, zinc and omega-3. The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics states that well-planned vegan diets are appropriate at all life stages.

angle.text: People go vegan for a leaner body and clearer skin, since higher fibre and lower saturated fat can lower weight and improve cardiometabolic markers. Trials cover weight and metabolic outcomes; skin and eye-colour claims are anecdotal.

vegetarian-pescatarian.summary: Reduced-meat diets, vegetarian or with fish, used for leanness, skin and general health, with population data on health outcomes.

quick.overview:
Vegetarian diets exclude meat and pescatarian diets add fish and seafood; both may include eggs and dairy. They are a moderate middle ground between omnivore and vegan eating, used for leanness, skin and general health.

The chain is a shift toward plants and, for pescatarians, fish-derived omega-3, which improves overall diet quality and can help body composition. Research is observational: a UK Biobank cohort and meta-analysis looked at cancer risk, a Swiss population study at cardiovascular risk factors, and studies of young people compared micronutrient status. None test appearance.
quick.how: People drop meat, keep eggs, dairy and fish to taste, and build meals around legumes, vegetables, grains and seafood. Many see it as an easier, flexible step than going fully vegan.
quick.risks: Nutrient studies compare B12, iron and others across diets, and vegetarians are advised to watch B12 and iron. Some fish carry mercury and PCBs.

angle.text: Vegetarian and pescatarian diets reduce meat and raise plant and fish intake, which people use to get leaner and support healthier skin. Population data cover health outcomes; looks are not directly studied.

mediterranean-diet.summary: Olive oil, vegetables, legumes and fish: the best-studied diet pattern, used as a baseline for general health, healthier skin and weight control.

quick.overview:
The Mediterranean diet is a plant-forward pattern built on olive oil, vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, fish and nuts, with limited red meat and sweets. People use it as an everyday baseline for healthier skin and a leaner body.

The chain is unsaturated fats, fibre and polyphenols improving overall health markers and gut microbiota, with weight control as a flow-on effect. It is among the best-studied patterns: the PREDIMED trial and Lyon Diet Heart Study examined cardiovascular outcomes, and a Greek cohort linked adherence to survival. Direct trials on skin or looks were not identified.
quick.how: Meals centre on vegetables, legumes, fish, whole grains and extra-virgin olive oil, with moderate dairy and poultry and wine with meals in the traditional version. People adopt it as a long-term way of eating rather than a short cycle.
quick.risks: Cost and nutrient gaps outside the original cultural settings have been noted, and moderate wine is part of the traditional pattern.

angle.text: People use the Mediterranean pattern as a well-researched baseline for general health, skin and weight control, through olive oil, plants and fish improving overall health markers. Cardiovascular evidence is strong; appearance is inferred rather than directly studied.

anti-inflammatory-diet.summary: Whole-food, low-processed eating aimed at lowering chronic inflammation, used for less facial puffiness and fewer breakouts.

quick.overview:
An anti-inflammatory diet emphasises fish, berries, greens, olive oil and nuts while limiting processed foods, refined carbohydrates, added sugar and red and processed meat. People in appearance communities use it for a less puffy face and fewer breakouts.

The chain is that omega-3s, polyphenols and fibre lower chronic low-grade inflammation, measured by markers such as CRP and IL-6, which followers link to less puffiness and acne. The Mediterranean diet is commonly given as the model. Research examines inflammation markers and diet indices, mostly for heart disease, bowel disease, depression and cognitive health, and no trials were found on facial puffiness or acne.
quick.how: People fill plates with fish, berries, leafy greens, olive oil and nuts, and cut back on processed foods and sugar. It is run as a long-term eating pattern, and users report on skin and puffiness over weeks to months.
quick.risks: It is a conventional food pattern, and sources advise discussing individual conditions with a clinician.

angle.text: Users eat whole, low-processed foods to lower chronic inflammation, with less facial puffiness and fewer breakouts as the payoff. Research tracks inflammation markers and disease outcomes rather than puffiness or acne directly.

dairy-free-for-skin.summary: Cutting milk, and sometimes all dairy, for fewer breakouts and a less puffy face, based on observational links between dairy and acne.

quick.overview:
Dairy-free for skin means giving up milk, and sometimes all dairy, hoping for fewer breakouts and a less puffy face. It is a common suggestion in skincare and looksmaxxing discussions.

The proposed chain is that milk contains whey protein and hormones, including bovine IGF-1 and precursors of dihydrotestosterone, which could amplify insulin and IGF-1 signaling, androgen production, sebum output and comedone formation. Wikipedia's acne article describes weak observational evidence that milk consumption is associated with more frequent and severe acne, and states that evidence was insufficient to recommend milk restriction as of 2014. No trial results are summarized for facial puffiness.
quick.how: People drop milk first, sometimes all dairy, and swap in plant milks or other foods. Users usually judge it over several weeks of skin changes.
quick.risks: No safety issues with dairy elimination were identified in the sources used. Milk is a source of nutrients, and people who remove it generally need to replace them from other foods.

angle.text: People avoid milk and sometimes other dairy to clear acne and, in some accounts, reduce facial puffiness, on the idea that milk hormones raise oil production. Observational studies link milk to acne weakly, and trials are lacking.

no-sugar-sugar-free-lifestyle.summary: Avoiding added sugar for clearer, younger-looking skin and a leaner body, in line with health guidance to eat less sugar.

quick.overview:
A no-sugar lifestyle means avoiding added and free sugars, with the aim of clearer skin, slower skin ageing and a leaner body. It is a frequent theme in skincare and looksmaxxing talk.

For acne, the proposed chain is that high blood sugar and insulin raise IGF-1 and androgen activity, so lower sugar means fewer breakouts. Believers also point to glycation, where sugars bind to proteins such as collagen, as a route to ageing skin. Public health bodies recommend limiting free sugars, and Wikipedia reports dermatologists suggest a diet low in simple sugars for acne.
quick.how: People cut sweets, sugary drinks and sweetened foods, read labels for added sugar, and often replace them with whole foods. Skin changes are usually judged over weeks.
quick.risks: Cutting sugar is a mainstream dietary change. Extreme versions that remove whole food groups can affect nutrition.

angle.text: Users cut added sugar for clearer, younger-looking skin and a leaner body, through lower blood sugar swings and less glycation. Health guidelines support eating less sugar; skin-specific trials are thin.

gluten-free-for-skin.summary: Avoiding wheat, barley and rye for clearer skin: essential for celiac-linked rashes, with no acne trials found.

quick.overview:
Gluten-free for skin means avoiding wheat, barley and rye in the hope of clearer skin and less inflammation. It circulates widely in wellness and looksmaxxing spaces.

The chain believers describe is less gluten-driven gut and skin inflammation, so skin clears. In medical contexts the diet works for gluten-triggered autoimmune conditions: it is the established treatment for celiac disease and for the skin rash dermatitis herpetiformis. Wikipedia's acne article does not discuss gluten, and no acne-specific trials were found.
quick.how: People remove bread, pasta and other gluten grains and use gluten-free replacements or naturally gluten-free foods. Users typically judge skin over a few weeks to months.
quick.risks: Poorly chosen replacements can cause nutritional gaps such as lower iron and B vitamins and more sugar and saturated fat. Clinicians advise testing for celiac disease before starting the diet.

angle.text: Some people go gluten-free hoping to clear acne and calm skin inflammation. It is the standard treatment for celiac-linked rashes; no acne trials were found for people without those conditions.

low-sodium-for-face-de-puffing.summary: Cutting salt to reduce facial water retention for a slimmer, more defined-looking face.

quick.overview:
This practice means lowering salt intake to reduce water retention and facial puffiness, a common tip in looksmaxxing communities for a leaner, more defined face.

The chain is that sodium is involved in the osmotic regulation of water in body tissues, so less sodium means less retained water. Health guidance supports lower sodium for blood pressure, with the WHO recommending under 2,000 mg of sodium a day, about 5 g of salt. The sources reviewed do not discuss facial puffiness, and Wikipedia's acne article states evidence does not support a link between salt and acne.
quick.how: People cut processed and restaurant foods, season less, and read labels for sodium. Users report on morning facial puffiness within days to weeks.
quick.risks: Wikipedia notes the association between sodium intake and cardiovascular disease or mortality may be U-shaped, with risk at both high and low intakes.

angle.text: Users lower salt intake to reduce water retention and look slimmer and more defined in the face. Low sodium lowers blood pressure, and facial effects are not covered in the sources reviewed.
